chapters.title: The Ferry in Winter
chapters.summary: Mara, a night-shift nursing student, and her uncle Teodor, a ferry mechanic, shared a cold flat above the harbour while the news arrived in fragments through radios and phone screens. Ines, their neighbour, kept the building together with tea and stories. A stranger on the morning ferry began to appear too often, always reading, always leaving the paper behind. By the end of January Mara had started keeping the papers, and Teodor had stopped asking why.

chapters.title: Rent and Weather
chapters.summary: February brought a rent rise that Teodor could not cover and a storm that kept the ferries in port for a week. Mara took extra shifts and found a name written in the margin of one of the stranger's newspapers. Ines fell ill and recovered, though she now forgot the endings of her stories. On the last night of the month, Mara followed the stranger off the ferry and lost him in the fog behind the fish market, holding a key that was not hers.

days.sentence: Mara left the clinic after midnight, the interest story still on her phone, and on the tram she heard two men argue about the grain, the flu and the housing until her stop, where the harbour posters had faded.
Nobody at the harbour mentioned the smoke or the blackout, but Mara noticed how the old men went quiet when the screen above the bar showed the penalties, then the border, then the subsidy.
Mara counted the hours of her night shift by the bulletins: the ceasefire at ten, the coffee at eleven, the antibiotic at midnight, the shipwreck at one, and the flood just before dawn.
The landlord raised the rent and blamed the crew, the train and the spy, and Teodor, who had heard it all before, blamed the strike and then, quietly, the teachers.
In the kitchen Ines spread the newspaper over the table, so the quota and the monsoon soaked up the spilled tea, and the chip, the volcano and the lithium were folded away with the bread.
Teodor wrote Mara a letter he never sent, about the exam and the marathon, about the bronzes he remembered from boyhood, and about how the piracy and the villages made everything feel temporary.
On the ferry Mara watched a stranger read about the Arctic, fold the paper at the recount, frown at the comet, and leave it on the seat, open at the glacier and the opera.
Teodor fixed the ferry engine by lamplight while the radio drifted from the grain to the flu, and he thought of his sister, of the housing, of the harbour and, for no reason at all, of the snowstorm.
That evening the three of them ate on the balcony and said nothing about the blackout, the penalties, the border or the subsidy, though the satellite glowed on every screen across the street.
Ines told the neighbour's children a story in which the coffee, the antibiotic and the shipwreck were only the names of streets, and the flood and the coral were two dogs who never learned to sit.
